## Object

`VTask.smash` concatenates two consecutive relation series into a single longer series. Given a series `p` of the form `a₀ →r a₁ →r … →r X` and a series `q` of the form `X →r b₁ →r … →r bₙ`, it produces the combined series `a₀ →r … →r X →r b₁ →r … →r bₙ`. The junction point `X` appears exactly once in the combined series (it is not duplicated), so the total length is the sum of the two individual lengths.

## Signature

`{α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (p q : RelSeries r) -> (connect : p.last = q.head) -> RelSeries r`

The implicit type argument `α` is the carrier type of all elements in the series; `r` is the binary relation that must hold between consecutive elements. The argument `p` is the first (left) series, whose last element must equal the first element of the second series. The argument `q` is the second (right) series, which begins at the element where `p` ends. The proof `connect` witnesses that `p.last = q.head`, i.e., the two series share a common junction element.

## Conventions

The junction element `X = p.last = q.head` appears exactly once in the combined series: it occupies the position at index `p.length` (the last position of the `p`-segment) and is not repeated as the head of the `q`-segment. Consequently the length of the combined series equals `p.length + q.length` (not `p.length + q.length + 1`), reflecting the sharing of one element.

## Worked examples

- Claim: For any two composable series `p` and `q` with `p.last = q.head`, the length of `VTask.smash p q h` equals `p.length + q.length`.

- Claim: The values of `VTask.smash p q h` on indices belonging to the `p`-segment agree with the values of `p`. Specifically, for `i : Fin (p.length + 1)`, one has `(VTask.smash p q h) (i.castLE _) = p i`.

- Claim: The values of `VTask.smash p q h` on indices in the interior of the `q`-segment agree with `q`. Specifically, for `i : Fin q.length`, one has `(VTask.smash p q h) ((i.natAdd p.length).succ) = q i.succ`.

- Claim: The head of `VTask.smash p q h` equals the head of `p` (i.e., the combined series starts where `p` starts).

- Claim: The last element of `VTask.smash p q h` equals the last element of `q` (i.e., the combined series ends where `q` ends).

## Boundaries

- If `p` has length 0, then `p` consists of a single element which is simultaneously its head and last. The combined series is essentially `q` with its head relabelled to `p.last` (which equals `q.head` by hypothesis), so `VTask.smash p q h` has the same length as `q`.
- If `q` has length 0, the combined series has the same length as `p`, ending at `q.head = p.last`.
- Both `p` and `q` of length 0 yield a single-element series of length 0.
- The proof `connect` is required to be supplied explicitly; without evidence that the two series share a junction, concatenation is not defined.

## Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.append` (if it exists): a variant that might duplicate or not deduplicate the shared endpoint — `VTask.smash` specifically does not duplicate the junction element.
- Simple list concatenation: ordinary list/sequence concatenation of series with lengths `m` and `n` would yield length `m + n + 1` (since both endpoints are kept); `VTask.smash` yields length `m + n` by identifying the shared junction.
- `LTSeries.smash` or `LESeries.smash`: specialisations of this construction to series where `r` is `<` or `≤`; the operation is the same but the carrier relation is more constrained.

## Object

`VTask.pi` constructs, from a family of ring homomorphisms each mapping a common source ring `γ` into one of the factor rings `f i`, a single ring homomorphism from `γ` into the product ring `Π i, f i`. The resulting homomorphism sends each element `x : γ` to the tuple whose `i`-th component is the image of `x` under the `i`-th given homomorphism.

## Signature

```
VTask.pi : {I : Type u} -> {f : I → Type u_1} -> {γ : Type u_2} -> [(i : I) → NonAssocSemiring (f i)] -> [NonAssocSemiring γ] -> (g : (i : I) → γ →+* f i) -> γ →+* (i : I) → f i
```

`I` is the index type parametrising the family of factor rings. `f` assigns to each index `i : I` the corresponding factor ring type. `γ` is the common source (domain) ring. The typeclass `(i : I) → NonAssocSemiring (f i)` provides the semiring structure on each factor, and `NonAssocSemiring γ` provides the semiring structure on the source. The explicit argument `g` is the family of ring homomorphisms: for each index `i`, `g i` is a ring homomorphism from `γ` to `f i`. The output is a single ring homomorphism from `γ` to the product `Π i, f i`.

## Conventions

No special junk-value or boundary conventions are declared for this definition: it is a total construction taking well-typed inputs and always producing a valid ring homomorphism; there are no edge indices or degenerate inputs that require a special sentinel output.

## Worked examples

- Claim: For the family `g` consisting of the identity ring homomorphism on `ZMod 2` at every index `i : Fin 2`, `VTask.pi g` sends `1` to the tuple `(1, 1)`.

- Claim: The kernel of `VTask.pi g` equals the infimum (meet) of the kernels of the individual `g i`. That is, `x` maps to zero in every factor if and only if `x` is in all individual kernels simultaneously.

- Claim: If every `g i` is injective and `I` is nonempty, then `VTask.pi g` is injective.

- Claim: Evaluating `VTask.pi g` at an element `x : γ` and then projecting to coordinate `j` recovers `g j x`. In symbols, `(VTask.pi g x) j = g j x`.

## Boundaries

- When `I` is empty (`I = PEmpty` or `Fin 0`), the product `Π i, f i` is the trivial (terminal) ring, and `VTask.pi g` is the unique ring homomorphism into it; this is well-defined and requires no special casing.
- When `I` is a singleton, `VTask.pi g` is essentially the same as the single homomorphism `g` composed with the canonical isomorphism `f ⟨⟩ ≅ Π i, f i`.
- Injectivity of `VTask.pi g` requires the index type to be `Nonempty`; if every `g i` is injective the combined map is injective, but this is a separate theorem rather than built into the construction.
- Surjectivity of `VTask.pi g` is not automatic; surjectivity of each `g i` does not suffice in general (it holds component-wise but the tuple map may lack surjectivity depending on the family).

## Not to be confused with

- `Pi.evalRingHom`: the projection ring homomorphism `(Π i, f i) →+* f j` going in the opposite direction — it evaluates a tuple at a single index, rather than assembling a tuple from components.
- `NonUnitalRingHom.pi`: the analogous construction for non-unital ring homomorphisms; it has the same pointwise behaviour but lives in the category of non-unital rings and requires weaker typeclass hypotheses.
- `RingHom.prod`: the binary product variant `γ →+* α × β` built from two homomorphisms `γ →+* α` and `γ →+* β`; it is the special case `I = Fin 2` but is stated separately for the binary product type.

## Object

`VTask.Forall p l` is the proposition asserting that every element of the list `l` satisfies the predicate `p`. It is the list-indexed version of universal quantification, and unfolds directly to a finite conjunction: for example, on a three-element list `[a, b, c]` it reduces to `p a ∧ p b ∧ p c`, and on the empty list it is `True`.

## Signature

`{α : Type u_1} -> (p : α → Prop) -> List α → Prop`

The implicit type argument `α` is the element type of the list. The argument `p` is the predicate that must hold for each element. The final argument is the list whose elements are being checked.

## Conventions

On the empty list the proposition is `True`, representing the vacuously true universal statement. On a singleton list `[x]` it reduces to `p x` directly (no conjunction wrapper). On a list with two or more elements `x :: l` it reduces to `p x ∧ VTask.Forall p l`.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) [1, 2, 3]` is definitionally equal to `1 < 10 ∧ 2 < 10 ∧ 3 < 10`.

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) []` is definitionally equal to `True`.

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) [5]` is definitionally equal to `5 < 10`.

- Claim: If `∀ x, p x → q x` and `VTask.Forall p l`, then `VTask.Forall q l` (monotonicity under implication).

## Boundaries

- **Empty list**: `VTask.Forall p [] = True`, vacuously satisfied regardless of `p`.
- **Singleton list**: `VTask.Forall p [x] = p x`, with no extra conjunct — note the absence of a trailing `∧ True`.
- **Two or more elements**: behaves inductively as a right-associated conjunction `p x ∧ VTask.Forall p l`.
- The proposition is equivalent to `∀ a ∈ l, p a`, but the unfolding is a concrete conjunction rather than a bounded quantifier, which can affect definitional reduction and tactic behavior.

## Not to be confused with

- `List.Forall₂`: a *binary* relation lifted pointwise across two lists of the same length; involves two lists, not one.
- `∀ a ∈ l, p a`: logically equivalent bounded quantifier form, but does not reduce definitionally to a conjunction.
- `List.all`: a `Bool`-valued decision procedure for membership-style checks, not a `Prop`.

## Object

The hyperoperation sequence is a family of binary operations on the natural numbers, indexed by a level `n`, that extends the usual arithmetic hierarchy: level 0 is the successor function, level 1 is addition, level 2 is multiplication, level 3 is exponentiation, and each higher level is defined by iterated application of the previous level. Formally, `VTask.hyperoperation n m k` computes the `n`-th hyperoperation applied to operands `m` (the base) and `k` (the height or exponent analogue).

## Signature

`VTask.hyperoperation : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`

The first argument `n` is the level of the hyperoperation (0 = successor, 1 = addition, 2 = multiplication, 3 = exponentiation, 4 = tetration, etc.). The second argument `m` is the left operand (base). The third argument `k` is the right operand (height or iterated count).

## Conventions

At level 0, the left operand `m` is completely ignored, and the result is always `k + 1` (the successor of `k`). At level 1 with right operand 0, the result is `m` (addition base case: `m + 0 = m`). At level 2 with right operand 0, the result is 0 (multiplication base case: `m * 0 = 0`). At level 3 and above with right operand 0, the result is 1 (exponentiation base case: `m ^ 0 = 1`, and all higher operations similarly return 1 for right operand 0). For any operand `m` and any level `n ≥ 3`, applying the `n`-th hyperoperation with left operand 1 always returns 1 regardless of the right operand.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 0 5 3 = 4` — level 0 ignores `m` and returns `k + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 1 3 4 = 7` — level 1 is addition, so `3 + 4 = 7`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 2 3 4 = 12` — level 2 is multiplication, so `3 * 4 = 12`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 3 2 10 = 1024` — level 3 is exponentiation, so `2 ^ 10 = 1024`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 16` — level 4 is tetration; `2 ↑↑ 3 = 2^(2^2) = 2^4 = 16`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 5 1 100 = 1` — for level `n ≥ 3`, the left operand `m = 1` always gives result 1.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 3 0 0 = 1` — level 3 with right operand 0 gives 1 (base case for exponentiation: `0 ^ 0 = 1` in this convention).

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 2 7 1 = 7` — at level 2 and above, right operand 1 returns `m` (since `m * 1 = m`).

## Boundaries

- At level 0, the middle argument `m` is entirely irrelevant; `VTask.hyperoperation 0 m k = k + 1` for all `m` and `k`.
- At level 1 and above, the right operand `k = 0` triggers a level-specific base case: level 1 returns `m`, level 2 returns 0, and all levels ≥ 3 return 1.
- At level 2 and above, the right operand `k = 1` always returns `m` (the left operand), matching the identity element behaviour (e.g., `m * 1 = m`, `m ^ 1 = m`).
- For levels ≥ 4, with left operand 0 and right operand `k`, the result alternates: it is 1 when `k` is even and 0 when `k` is odd.
- For left operand `m = 1` at levels ≥ 3, the result is always 1 regardless of `k`, because iterated application of `1` under any hyperoperation collapses to 1.
- The function is total on all natural numbers; there are no undefined or out-of-domain inputs.

## Not to be confused with

- Natural number exponentiation `Nat.pow m k` — that is exactly `VTask.hyperoperation 3 m k`, just the third level, not the full sequence.
- Ackermann's function — closely related and similarly fast-growing, but defined differently (with a different index convention and using subtraction in the recursive step).
- Iterated function application `Nat.iterate f n` — a general combinator for applying a function `n` times, which can be used to build hyperoperations but is not the same object.

### Object

Given two finite relational series — a chain `a₀ -r→ a₁ -r→ … -r→ X` of length `m` and a chain `X -r→ b₁ -r→ … -r→ bₙ` of length `n` that begins exactly where the first one ends — `VTask.smash` produces a single concatenated relational series `a₀ -r→ a₁ -r→ … -r→ X -r→ b₁ -r→ … -r→ bₙ` of length `m + n`. The junction point `X` appears exactly once in the concatenated series (it is not duplicated).

### Signature

The implicit argument `α` is the carrier type whose elements form the nodes of the series, and `r` is the binary relation that must hold between consecutive elements. The argument `p` is the first (left) series, ending at some element `X`. The argument `q` is the second (right) series, beginning at that same element `X`. The argument `connect` is a proof that the last element of `p` equals the head (first element) of `q`, certifying that the two series share their junction point and may be legally joined.

### Conventions

There are no junk-value conventions for this definition: the function is total and defined only when the compatibility condition `connect : p.last = q.head` is explicitly supplied by the caller. No out-of-range or degenerate input is silently extended or defaulted.

### Worked examples

- Claim: The length of `VTask.smash p q h` equals `p.length + q.length`.

- Claim: For any index `i : Fin (p.length + 1)` in the left portion, `VTask.smash p q h` evaluated at the corresponding index equals `p i` (the value at that position in `p`).

- Claim: For any index `i : Fin q.length`, the element of `VTask.smash p q h` at the position corresponding to `i.succ` in the right block equals `q i.succ`.

- Claim: The head of `VTask.smash p q h` equals the head of `p`, and the last element equals the last element of `q`.

- If `p` has length 0 (a single-element series consisting only of `X`) and `q` also has length 0, then `VTask.smash p q h` has length 0 and is itself a single-element series equal to `X`.

- The index type of `VTask.smash p q h` is `Fin (p.length + q.length + 1)`, which naturally decomposes into a left block of size `p.length + 1` (indices `0` through `p.length`) and a right block of size `q.length + 1` (indices `p.length` through `p.length + q.length`), with index `p.length` corresponding to the shared junction element `X`.

## VTask.StrictMonoOn

### Object

`VTask.StrictMonoOn f s` is the proposition that the function `f` is *strictly monotone on the set `s`*: whenever two elements `a` and `b` both belong to `s` and `a` is strictly less than `b` (in the preorder on the domain), their images satisfy `f a < f b` (in the preorder on the codomain). This is the set-restricted version of global strict monotonicity.

### Signature

`VTask.StrictMonoOn : {α : Type u} -> {β : Type v} -> [Preorder α] -> [Preorder β] -> (f : α → β) -> (s : Set α) -> Prop`

The universe-polymorphic type parameters `α` and `β` are the domain and codomain types, respectively. The two `Preorder` instances supply the strict-order relations `<` on both types. The explicit argument `f` is the function whose monotonicity is being asserted. The explicit argument `s` is the subset of the domain on which the monotonicity condition is imposed; elements outside `s` are entirely ignored.

### Conventions

There are no junk-value or out-of-domain conventions to declare: `VTask.StrictMonoOn` is a universally quantified proposition over all pairs in `s`, so for any inputs it is a well-formed `Prop`. When `s` is empty or a singleton, the universal quantification is vacuously satisfied (see Boundaries).

### Worked examples

- Claim: The function `fun n : ℕ => n + 1` is strictly monotone on the set `{1, 2, 3}`.

- Claim: The identity function on `ℝ` is strictly monotone on any interval `Set.Ioi 0`.

- Claim: A constant function is **not** strictly monotone on any set containing at least two distinct elements, because `a < b` in the domain would require `f a < f b`, but `f a = f b`.

- Claim: `VTask.StrictMonoOn (fun n : ℕ => 2 * n) Set.univ` holds, since for all natural numbers `a < b` implies `2 * a < 2 * b`.

### Boundaries

- **Empty set**: When `s = ∅`, the proposition holds vacuously for every function `f`, since no pair `(a, b)` with both `a ∈ s` and `b ∈ s` exists.
- **Singleton set**: When `s = {x}` for a single element `x`, the condition is again vacuously true: there is no pair with `a < b` both in `s`.
- **Two-element set**: With `s = {a, b}` and `a < b`, the condition reduces to the single requirement `f a < f b`.
- **The whole type (`s = Set.univ`)**: `VTask.StrictMonoOn f Set.univ` is equivalent to global `StrictMono f`.
- **Non-strict vs strict**: The predicate uses strict inequality `<` in both domain and codomain; a weakly monotone function that maps two distinct elements to equal values does *not* satisfy it.

### Not to be confused with

- **`StrictMono f`**: The global version; equivalent to `VTask.StrictMonoOn f Set.univ` but does not carry a set argument.
- **`MonoOn f s`** (a.k.a. `Set.MapsTo`-style monotonicity): The *non-strict* (weak) version requires only `a ≤ b → f a ≤ f b` on `s`, which is weaker than `VTask.StrictMonoOn`.
- **`StrictAntiOn f s`**: The strict *anti*-monotone counterpart, requiring `a < b → f b < f a` for elements of `s`; the ordering in the codomain is reversed.

## 1. Object

Given a predicate `p` on elements of type `α` and a list `l` of elements of type `α`, this proposition asserts that `p` holds for every element of `l`. It is logically equivalent to `∀ a ∈ l, p a`, but it unfolds structurally into a finite iterated conjunction rather than a universally quantified membership statement. For example, on a three-element list `[a, b, c]` it reduces to `p a ∧ p b ∧ p c`, and on the empty list it reduces to `True`.

## 2. Signature

VTask.Forall : {α : Type u_1} -> (p : α → Prop) -> List α → Prop

The implicit type argument `α` is the element type shared by the predicate and the list. The argument `p` is the unary predicate to be checked against every element. The final argument is the list whose elements are to be tested.

## 3. Conventions

On the empty list the proposition is `True`, reflecting the vacuous truth of "every element satisfies `p`" when there are no elements.

## 4. Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) [1, 2, 3]` holds, since each of 1, 2, 3 is less than 10, reducing to `(1 < 10) ∧ (2 < 10) ∧ (3 < 10)`.

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) []` holds, since the empty-list case reduces to `True`.

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n > 5) [1, 2, 3]` does not hold, since 1 is not greater than 5; the conjunction `(1 > 5) ∧ (2 > 5) ∧ (3 > 5)` is false.

- Claim: For a singleton list `[a]`, `VTask.Forall p [a]` is definitionally equal to `p a` (no conjunction wrapper is introduced for a single element).

## 5. Boundaries

- **Empty list**: `VTask.Forall p [] = True` — the proposition holds trivially with no conditions.
- **Singleton list**: `VTask.Forall p [x] = p x` — no conjunction is produced; the result is exactly `p x`.
- **Two or more elements**: `VTask.Forall p (x :: l) = (p x ∧ VTask.Forall p l)` when `l` is nonempty — the result is a right-associated conjunction.
- The predicate `p` is arbitrary; no well-formedness conditions are imposed on it.

## 6. Not to be confused with

- `List.Forall₂`: a binary relation lifted to two lists element-wise (relates corresponding positions of two lists), not a single predicate over one list.
- `∀ a ∈ l, p a`: the membership-quantified form, logically equivalent but does not reduce to a bare conjunction and behaves differently under `simp`/`decide`.
- `List.All`: a boolean-valued function checking a decidable predicate on all elements, not a `Prop`-valued conjunction.

## Object

The hyperoperation sequence is a family of binary operations on natural numbers, indexed by a level `n`, that generalises successor, addition, multiplication, and exponentiation in a single recursive scheme. At level 0 it is the successor function; at level 1, addition; at level 2, multiplication; at level 3, exponentiation; and for each higher level, iterated application of the previous level. The sequence grows extraordinarily fast: level 4 is tetration, level 5 is pentation, and so on.

## Signature

VTask.hyperoperation : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ

The first argument `n` selects the level of the operation in the hierarchy (0 = successor, 1 = addition, 2 = multiplication, 3 = exponentiation, …). The second argument `m` is the left operand (the "base" in exponential language, the repeated element in iterated operations). The third argument `k` is the right operand (the number of times to iterate the next-lower operation).

## Conventions

At level 0 the left operand `m` is ignored entirely; the result is always `k + 1` regardless of `m`. At level 1 with right operand 0 the result is `m` (addition identity: `m + 0 = m`). At level 2 with right operand 0 the result is 0 (multiplication by zero). For every level 3 and above with right operand 0 the result is 1 (the iterated-exponentiation identity: the empty iterated product is 1). For every level 3 and above with left operand 1 the result is 1 (any tower of 1s is 1). The right-operand-1 identity for levels 2 and above returns `m` unchanged (`m * 1 = m`, `m ^ 1 = m`, etc.).

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 0 99 7 = 8` — level 0 is successor; the left operand is ignored and the result is `k + 1 = 8`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 1 3 4 = 7` — level 1 is addition; `3 + 4 = 7`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 2 5 6 = 30` — level 2 is multiplication; `5 × 6 = 30`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 3 2 10 = 1024` — level 3 is exponentiation; `2 ^ 10 = 1024`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 16` — level 4 is tetration; `2 ↑↑ 3 = 2^(2^2) = 16`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 6 1 999 = 1` — for any level ≥ 3, left operand 1 always yields 1.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 5 2 2 = 4` — for any level ≥ 1, `VTask.hyperoperation n 2 2 = 4`.

## Boundaries

- **Level 0, any `m`, any `k`:** returns `k + 1`; the left operand plays no role whatsoever.
- **Level 1, `k = 0`:** returns `m` (addition by zero).
- **Level 2, `k = 0`:** returns `0` (multiplication by zero).
- **Level ≥ 3, `k = 0`:** returns `1` (empty tower convention).
- **Level ≥ 3, `m = 1`:** returns `1` for every right operand.
- **Level ≥ 2, `k = 1`:** returns `m` (the right-identity of each operation above addition).
- **`m = 2`, `k = 2`, level ≥ 1:** always returns `4`, no matter how high the level.
- **Level ≥ 4, `m = 0`, `k` even:** returns `1`; `k` odd: returns `0` (alternating pattern from the zero-base tower).

## Not to be confused with

- **`Nat.pow`** (or `HPow.hPow` on `ℕ`): ordinary exponentiation, which coincides with `VTask.hyperoperation 3 m k` but is not the general iterated-operation hierarchy.
- **Ackermann function**: closely related and grows at a similar rate, but is a different two-argument function; the hyperoperation sequence can be used to express it, but the two definitions are not identical.
- **`Nat.succ`**: the level-0 case of `VTask.hyperoperation` (applied to `k`) equals `Nat.succ k`, but `VTask.hyperoperation` takes three arguments and is not the successor function itself.

The argument `hx` is a proof that `x` satisfies the chain condition: for every pair of adjacent elements in the list, the relation `r` holds between them.

### Object

`VTask.StrictAntiOn f s` is the proposition that the function `f` is *strictly antitone* (strictly order-reversing) when restricted to the set `s`. Concretely, it asserts that for any two elements `a` and `b` both belonging to `s`, whenever `a` is strictly less than `b` in the domain's order, the image `f b` is strictly less than `f a` in the codomain's order — that is, `f` strictly reverses the ordering on `s`.

### Signature

The implicit type parameters `α` and `β` are the domain and codomain types, respectively. The instance arguments supply preorders on both types, giving meaning to the strict inequality symbols `<`. The explicit argument `f` is the function whose monotonicity behaviour is being examined. The explicit argument `s` is the subset of the domain to which the strict antitonicity condition is confined.

### Conventions

No special junk-value or boundary conventions are declared: the predicate is a universally quantified statement over pairs from `s`, so on an empty set or a singleton set the hypothesis `a < b` is vacuously unsatisfiable and `VTask.StrictAntiOn f s` holds for every `f` regardless of what `f` does.

### Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.StrictAntiOn f (∅ : Set α)` holds for every function `f`, because there are no pairs in the empty set to check.

- Claim: `VTask.StrictAntiOn (fun x : ℝ => -x) Set.univ` — negation is strictly antitone on all of `ℝ`, since `a < b` implies `-b < -a`.

- Claim: `VTask.StrictAntiOn (fun x : ℝ => x⁻¹) (Set.Ioi 0)` — the reciprocal function is strictly antitone on the positive reals.

- Claim: If `hg : VTask.StrictAntiOn g t` and `hf : VTask.StrictAntiOn f s` and `hs : Set.MapsTo f s t`, then `VTask.StrictAntiOn (g ∘ f) s` does *not* hold in general; instead the composition of two strictly antitone functions is strictly *monotone* on `s`.

### Boundaries

- **Empty set**: `VTask.StrictAntiOn f ∅` is always true; the universal quantification has no witnesses.
- **Singleton set**: `VTask.StrictAntiOn f {a}` is always true; within a singleton, no strict inequality `a < b` holds.
- **Subsingleton set**: More generally, any subsingleton subset makes the predicate vacuously true.
- **All of `α`**: Restricting to `Set.univ` recovers the global strict antitonicity notion `StrictAnti f` (up to the subtype equivalence).
- **Injectivity**: A strictly antitone function on a set is automatically injective on that set.
- **Composition rule**: Composing two strictly antitone functions (with appropriate mapping conditions) yields a strictly *monotone* composition, not a strictly antitone one.

### Not to be confused with

- **`AntitoneOn f s`**: The non-strict version; `a < b` is replaced by `a ≤ b`, so `VTask.StrictAntiOn f s` is strictly stronger.
- **`StrictMonoOn f s`**: The strictly *order-preserving* counterpart; `a < b` implies `f a < f b` rather than `f b < f a`.
- **`StrictAnti f`**: The global (non-localised) version, asserting strict antitonicity on all of `α` rather than just on a subset `s`.

## Object

`VTask.map` is the pointwise-lifting operation on dependent functions: given a family of functions `f i : α i → β i` indexed by `i : ι`, it sends a dependent function `a : ∀ i, α i` to the dependent function that returns `f i (a i)` at each index `i`. In other words, it applies each `f i` fibrewise to the corresponding component of `a`.

## Signature

`VTask.map : {ι : Sort u_1} -> {α : ι → Sort u_2} -> {β : ι → Sort u_3} -> (f : (i : ι) → α i → β i) -> ((i : ι) → α i) → (i : ι) → β i`

The index type `ι` (implicit) is the domain over which all functions are indexed. The dependent type families `α` and `β` (implicit) assign a type to each index. The explicit argument `f` is a family of fibrewise maps, one per index. The explicit argument of type `(i : ι) → α i` is the dependent function being transformed.

## Conventions

There are no junk-value or edge conventions to declare: the operation is total and well-defined for all inputs, including when `ι` is empty (in which case both the input and output dependent functions are vacuously defined).

## Worked examples

- Claim: Applying `VTask.map` with `f i n := n + 1` (where `ι = Fin 3` and `α i = β i = ℕ`) to the constant-zero function yields the constant-one function.
  ```lean
  example : VTask.map (fun (_ : Fin 3) (n : ℕ) => n + 1) (fun _ => 0) = (fun _ => 1) := by
    funext i; fin_cases i <;> rfl
  ```

- Claim: Composing two applications of `VTask.map` with families `f` and `g` is the same as a single application of `VTask.map` with the pointwise-composed family `fun i => g i ∘ f i`.
  ```lean
  example {ι : Type} {α β γ : ι → Type}
      (f : ∀ i, α i → β i) (g : ∀ i, β i → γ i) (a : ∀ i, α i) :
      VTask.map g (VTask.map f a) = VTask.map (fun i => g i ∘ f i) a := by
    funext i; rfl
  ```

- Claim: When `f i` is the identity for every `i`, `VTask.map f a = a`.
  ```lean
  example {ι : Type} {α : ι → Type} (a : ∀ i, α i) :
      VTask.map (fun i => id) a = a := by
    funext i; rfl
  ```

## Boundaries

- When `ι` is an empty type (e.g., `Empty` or `Fin 0`), both the input and output are the unique empty dependent function. The result is trivially correct and well-typed.
- When `ι` is a singleton, `VTask.map` reduces to applying the single fibrewise function to the single value.
- When `α i = β i` and each `f i` is the identity, `VTask.map f` is definitionally equal to the identity on `∀ i, α i`.
- The operation does not require `ι` to be a `Type`; it works for any `Sort`, including `Prop`.

## Not to be confused with

- `Function.comp`: ordinary function composition for non-dependent functions; `VTask.map` is the dependent generalisation operating pointwise over a whole family of types.
- The categorical `Pi.map` in `CategoryTheory.Limits.Shapes.Products`: that is a morphism between categorical product objects and lives in a category, whereas `VTask.map` operates purely on set-theoretic dependent functions.
- `Function.update`: modifies a dependent function at a single specified index rather than uniformly transforming every index.

## Object

`VTask.xor` computes the bitwise XOR of two integers. The operation extends the familiar bitwise XOR from natural numbers to all integers by using the two's-complement representation: non-negative integers are represented by their binary digits, and negative integers are represented in the "one's-complement-shifted" style where −(n+1) carries the bitwise pattern of n. Under this convention the k-th bit of the result is the Boolean XOR of the k-th bits of the two inputs, for every bit position k.

## Signature

`VTask.xor : ℤ → ℤ → ℤ`

The first argument is the left integer operand; the second argument is the right integer operand. Both are arbitrary integers (no sign restriction).

## Conventions

The function uses a two's-complement–style encoding: a negative integer −(n+1) for n : ℕ carries the bit pattern of the natural number n. Accordingly when both arguments are non-negative the result is also non-negative and equals the natural-number XOR; when exactly one argument is negative the result is negative; and when both arguments are negative the result is non-negative. This sign rule mirrors the two's-complement identity that negating flips all bits, so XOR-ing two "all-flipped" patterns yields an unflipped pattern.

## Worked examples

- Claim: VTask.xor 6 3 = 5 (both non-negative: 110 XOR 011 = 101)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.xor 6 3 = 5 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: VTask.xor 0 0 = 0 (XOR of zero with itself is zero)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.xor 0 0 = 0 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: VTask.xor (-3) (-5) = 6 (both negative: (−3)=−[2+1], (−5)=−[4+1]; 2 XOR 4 = 6)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.xor (-3) (-5) = 6 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: VTask.xor 5 (-3) = -7 (mixed signs: 5 XOR 2 = 7, result is −[6+1] = −7)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.xor 5 (-3) = -7 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: VTask.xor m n = VTask.xor n m for all integers m n (commutativity)

- Claim: The k-th bit of VTask.xor m n equals the Boolean XOR of the k-th bits of m and n

## Boundaries

- When both arguments are 0, the result is 0.
- When one argument is 0 and the other is any integer x, the result is x (0 is the identity element for bitwise XOR).
- When both arguments are the same integer x, the result is 0 (every bit XOR'd with itself cancels).
- When exactly one argument is negative, the result is always negative; when both are negative, the result is always non-negative.
- There are no restrictions on input magnitude; the function is total over all of ℤ.

## Not to be confused with

- `Bool.xor` / `Nat.xor` (`^^^`): the Boolean or natural-number XOR; `VTask.xor` extends this to integers with a sign convention.
- `Xor` (the logical connective): the propositional "exclusive or" on `Prop`, entirely unrelated to bitwise operations.
- `Int.bitwise`: a general bitwise combinator parameterised by an arbitrary Boolean function; `VTask.xor` is the specific instance where that function is `Bool.xor`.

## VTask.extend

### Object

Given a finpartition `P` of an element `a` in a modular lattice with a bottom element, and given a nonzero element `b` that is disjoint from `a`, `VTask.extend` produces a finpartition of `c = a ⊔ b` by adding `b` as one new part alongside all the existing parts of `P`. Informally: if you have already cut `a` into pairwise-disjoint pieces whose join is `a`, and `b` is a fresh nonzero piece disjoint from `a`, then the collection consisting of `b` together with all pieces of `P` is a valid partition of `a ⊔ b`.

### Signature

```
VTask.extend : {α : Type u_1} -> [Lattice α] -> [OrderBot α] -> [IsModularLattice α] -> [DecidableEq α] -> {a b c : α} -> (P : Finpartition a) -> (hb : b ≠ ⊥) -> (hab : Disjoint a b) -> (hc : a ⊔ b = c) -> Finpartition c
```

The implicit type `α` is the carrier of the modular lattice. The typeclass arguments supply lattice operations, a bottom element `⊥`, the modular law (needed for the independent-sup condition), and decidable equality on `α` (needed to work with finite sets of parts). The argument `P` is the finpartition of `a` being extended. The argument `hb` is proof that the new piece `b` is not the bottom element (ensuring `b` is a genuine part). The argument `hab` is proof that `b` and `a` are disjoint (ensuring the new piece does not overlap any existing part). The argument `hc` equates the join `a ⊔ b` with the target element `c`, so the result is declared as a finpartition of `c`.

### Conventions

The output element `c` is given as an explicit parameter via the equation `hc : a ⊔ b = c` rather than simply setting `c = a ⊔ b`; this allows `c` to be a pre-existing name in the context instead of forcing `a ⊔ b` syntactically. When `a ⊔ b` is the desired target, one may pass `rfl` for `hc`.

### Worked examples

- Claim: The parts of `VTask.extend P hb hab hc` are exactly `insert b P.parts`.

- Claim: For any finpartition `P` of `a`, `#(VTask.extend P hb hab hc).parts = #P.parts + 1`. (This is the content of `Finpartition.card_extend`: extending by a disjoint nonzero element strictly increases the number of parts by exactly one.)

- Claim: The element `b` is a member of the parts of `VTask.extend P hb hab hc`. (Since the new parts are `insert b P.parts`, `b` belongs to this set by `Finset.mem_insert_self`.)

- Claim: Every part of the original `P` is also a part of `VTask.extend P hb hab hc`. (The original parts are a subset of `insert b P.parts`, so membership is preserved under extension.)

### Boundaries

- The hypothesis `hb : b ≠ ⊥` is essential: if `b = ⊥` were allowed, `⊥` would become a part, violating the finpartition invariant that `⊥` is not a part.
- The hypothesis `hab : Disjoint a b` is essential: without it, `b` would overlap some existing part, breaking the pairwise-disjointness (independent-sup) requirement.
- If `a = ⊥` (i.e., `P` is the empty partition of `⊥`), the construction still works: the result is the single-part partition `{b}` of `b`, provided `b ≠ ⊥`.
- The modular lattice hypothesis is used to verify the sup-independence condition for the extended set of parts; the construction would not in general be valid in a non-modular lattice.
- The element `c` need not be named differently from `a ⊔ b`; passing `hc := rfl` (when `c` is definitionally `a ⊔ b`) is a common use pattern.

### Not to be confused with

- `Finpartition.extendOfLE`: extends a finpartition to a larger element by computing the set-difference piece, rather than requiring the user to supply the extra piece explicitly.
- `Finpartition.bind`: refines or coarsens a finpartition by replacing each part with a sub-partition, a structurally different operation.
- `Finpartition.indiscrete`: the trivial single-part partition of a nonzero element, not an extension of any existing partition.

## Object

`VTask.strongInductionOn` is the **strong induction principle** (also called well-founded induction by cardinality) for multisets. Given a predicate `p` on multisets, it allows one to prove `p s` for any multiset `s` by assuming, as an inductive hypothesis, that `p t` holds for every multiset `t` that is *strictly smaller* than `s` (i.e., `t < s` in the multiset ordering, which here amounts to `t` being a strict submultiset of `s` or having strictly smaller cardinality). This mirrors the classical principle: to prove a property of every multiset, it suffices to prove it for each multiset assuming it for all strictly smaller ones.

## Signature

`VTask.strongInductionOn : {α : Type u_1} -> {p : Multiset α → Sort u_3} -> (s : Multiset α) -> (ih : (s : Multiset α) → ((t : Multiset α) → t < s → p t) → p s) -> p s`

The implicit type argument `α` is the element type of the multisets. The implicit argument `p` is the motive — a type-valued (or sort-valued) predicate on multisets over `α` that one wishes to establish. The explicit argument `s` is the particular multiset for which one wants to derive `p s`. The explicit argument `ih` is the inductive step: a function that, for any multiset `s`, produces a proof (or inhabitant) of `p s` given a function that supplies `p t` for any `t` strictly less than `s`.

## Conventions

There are no junk-value or boundary conventions to declare for this induction combinator: it is well-defined and meaningful for every multiset `s` and every motive `p`, including the empty multiset (where the strict-smallness hypothesis is vacuously unavailable, so `ih` must produce the result without any inductive call).

## Worked examples

- Claim: Applying `VTask.strongInductionOn` to the empty multiset `(0 : Multiset ℕ)` with an inductive step `ih` reduces to `ih 0 (fun t ht => absurd ht (not_lt_of_le (le_refl 0)))`, i.e., the result equals `ih 0` applied to the (vacuously satisfied) hypothesis, since no multiset is strictly smaller than `∅`.

- Claim: For a multiset `s = {a}` (a singleton), the inductive hypothesis available inside `ih` can supply values only for the empty multiset `∅`, since `∅` is the only multiset strictly smaller than `{a}`.

- Claim: The unfolding equation holds — for any `s` and `ih`, the value `VTask.strongInductionOn s ih` equals `ih s (fun t _ => VTask.strongInductionOn t ih)`, meaning the combinator satisfies an immediate fixed-point equation that characterises its computational behaviour.

## Boundaries

- **Empty multiset**: When `s = ∅`, no multiset satisfies `t < ∅`, so the inner hypothesis function `(fun t ht => ...)` is never actually called. The result is entirely determined by `ih ∅` applied to a function with an empty domain.
- **Termination**: The recursion is well-founded because the multiset strict-order `<` is well-founded (every descending chain is finite), ensuring this combinator always terminates and is total.
- **Sort generality**: The motive `p` may range over any `Sort u_3`, including `Prop`, `Type`, or `Type*`, making this usable for both proof construction and type-level computation.

## Not to be confused with

- `Multiset.case_strongInductionOn`: A variant that splits the induction into a base case (empty multiset) and a cons step where the hypothesis is `∀ t ≤ s, p t` rather than strict inequality; useful when a cleaner case split is desired.
- `Multiset.induction_on` (simple structural induction on multisets): Only provides the result for strictly smaller multisets built by removing one element, rather than *all* strictly smaller multisets.
- `WellFounded.recursion` or `WellFounded.induction`: The general well-founded recursion/induction combinator for any `WellFoundedRelation`; `VTask.strongInductionOn` is its specialisation to the strict multiset ordering.

## Object

`VTask.swapCore a b r` is the elementary transposition function on an arbitrary type with decidable equality. It maps an element `r` to `b` if `r` equals `a`, to `a` if `r` equals `b`, and leaves `r` unchanged otherwise. In other words, it is the underlying point-wise action of swapping two designated elements `a` and `b`.

## Signature

`VTask.swapCore : {α : Sort u_1} -> [DecidableEq α] -> (a b r : α) -> α`

The implicit universe-polymorphic type `α` is the type on which the swap operates; it carries an implicit `DecidableEq` instance so that equality checks are computable. The argument `a` is the first element of the pair being transposed; `b` is the second element of the pair being transposed; `r` is the input element whose image under the transposition is computed.

## Conventions

When `a` equals `b`, the function acts as the identity: `VTask.swapCore a a r = r` for all `r`. There are no junk values or out-of-domain inputs because the function is total on all of `α`.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.swapCore 1 2 1 = 2` (element equal to `a` maps to `b`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.swapCore 1 2 1 = 2 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.swapCore 1 2 2 = 1` (element equal to `b` maps to `a`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.swapCore 1 2 2 = 1 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.swapCore 1 2 3 = 3` (element equal to neither `a` nor `b` is fixed)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.swapCore 1 2 3 = 3 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.swapCore 5 5 3 = 3` (degenerate case: swapping an element with itself is the identity)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.swapCore 5 5 3 = 3 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: Applying `VTask.swapCore a b` twice is the identity: `VTask.swapCore a b (VTask.swapCore a b r) = r` (involutivity)

- Claim: Swapping `a` and `b` gives the same result as swapping `b` and `a`: `VTask.swapCore a b r = VTask.swapCore b a r` (commutativity in the pair)

## Boundaries

- When `r = a` and `r = b` simultaneously (i.e., `a = b = r`), the first branch fires and returns `b`, which equals `r`, so the function is still the identity in this degenerate case.
- When `a = b` but `r` is different from both, the second branch (`r = b`) is also false, so `r` is returned unchanged; the function is always the identity when `a = b`.
- The function is involutive: applying it twice always returns the original element.
- The function is symmetric in `a` and `b`: swapping `a` with `b` or `b` with `a` yields the same result.

## Not to be confused with

- `Equiv.swap`: the full `Equiv` (bijection) built from this helper, packaging the forward and inverse maps together with proof of bijectivity.
- A general permutation or cycle: `VTask.swapCore` only exchanges exactly two specified elements and fixes everything else; it is not an arbitrary permutation.
- `Function.update`: updates a function at a single point, whereas `VTask.swapCore` updates at two points simultaneously (swapping their values).

## Object

The hyperoperation sequence is a family of binary operations on the natural numbers, indexed by a level parameter `n`. At level 0 it is the successor function (applied to the right argument), at level 1 it is addition, at level 2 it is multiplication, at level 3 it is exponentiation, and for every level beyond that it yields a new, rapidly-growing operation (tetration, pentation, …). Each level-`n+1` operation is defined by iterating the level-`n` operation, mirroring how multiplication iterates addition and exponentiation iterates multiplication.

## Signature

`VTask.hyperoperation : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`

The first argument is the **level** of the operation (0 = successor, 1 = addition, 2 = multiplication, 3 = exponentiation, …). The second argument is the **left operand** `m`. The third argument is the **right operand** `k`.

## Conventions

At level 0 (successor), the left operand is ignored and the result is `k + 1`. At level 1 with right operand 0 the result is `m` (the additive identity convention: `m + 0 = m`). At level 2 with right operand 0 the result is `0` (the multiplicative identity convention: `m * 0 = 0`). At any level ≥ 3 with right operand 0 the result is `1` (the iterated-exponentiation identity: `m ^ 0 = 1`, and the corresponding right-identity for all higher levels is also 1). For levels ≥ 2, the right operand 1 acts as an identity: `VTask.hyperoperation (n+2) m 1 = m`. For left operand 1 at any level ≥ 3 the result is always `1`.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 0 7 4 = 5` (level 0 ignores left operand, returns `k + 1 = 5`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 0 7 4 = 5 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 1 3 4 = 7` (level 1 is addition: `3 + 4 = 7`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 1 3 4 = 7 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 2 3 4 = 12` (level 2 is multiplication: `3 * 4 = 12`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 2 3 4 = 12 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 3 2 10 = 1024` (level 3 is exponentiation: `2 ^ 10 = 1024`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 3 2 10 = 1024 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 16` (level 4 is tetration: `2 ↑↑ 3 = 2^(2^2) = 16`)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 16 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 5 1 99 = 1` (left operand 1 at any level ≥ 3 gives 1)
  ```lean
  example : VTask.hyperoperation 5 1 99 = 1 := by decide
  ```

## Boundaries

- **Right operand 0, level 0**: the left operand is ignored; result is `0 + 1 = 1`.
- **Right operand 0, level 1**: result is `m` (addition identity).
- **Right operand 0, level 2**: result is `0` (multiplication: `m * 0 = 0`).
- **Right operand 0, level ≥ 3**: result is always `1` regardless of the left operand (iterated-exponentiation identity).
- **Right operand 1, level ≥ 2**: result is always `m`; 1 is the right identity at all levels from multiplication upward.
- **Left operand 1, level ≥ 3**: result is always `1`; iterated exponentiation of 1 never escapes 1.
- **Left operand 0, level ≥ 4**: the result alternates between 1 (even right operand) and 0 (odd right operand).
- **Level 0 ignores the left operand entirely**: only `k` and the successor rule matter.

## Not to be confused with

- **`Nat.succ`**: only the level-0 case of `VTask.hyperoperation`, which discards the left argument entirely.
- **`HPow.hPow` (natural number power)**: corresponds only to level 3 of `VTask.hyperoperation`; the general function extends far beyond exponentiation.
- **Ackermann function**: closely related and grows at the same hyper-exponential rate, but has a different recursive structure and different argument conventions.

## VTask.fromListIsChain

### Object

Given a nonempty list whose consecutive elements are related by a binary relation `r`, `VTask.fromListIsChain` packages that list into a `RelSeries r`: a finite sequence of elements of type `α` in which each adjacent pair `(aᵢ, aᵢ₊₁)` belongs to `r`. The length of the resulting series is one less than the length of the list (matching the convention that a series of length `n` has `n+1` elements).

### Signature

`VTask.fromListIsChain : {α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (x : List α) -> (x_ne_nil : x ≠ []) -> (hx : List.IsChain (fun x1 x2 => (x1, x2) ∈ r) x) -> RelSeries r`

- `α` is the carrier type whose elements form the series, inferred implicitly.
- `r` is the binary relation on `α` (a subset of `α × α`) that must hold between consecutive elements; it is inferred implicitly.
- `x` is the list of elements that will become the underlying sequence of the series.
- `x_ne_nil` is the proof that `x` is nonempty, ensuring the series has at least one element.
- `hx` is the proof that consecutive elements of `x` are related by `r`, i.e., the list satisfies the chain condition with respect to `r`.

### Conventions

The length field of the resulting `RelSeries` is `x.length - 1` (natural number subtraction), so a singleton list produces a series of length 0 (a single element with no steps), a two-element list produces a series of length 1, and so on.

### Worked examples

- Claim: For a singleton list `[a]`, `VTask.fromListIsChain [a] (by simp) (by simp [List.IsChain])` has length 0, i.e., the series consists of exactly one element.

- Claim: The `toList` of `VTask.fromListIsChain l hl_ne hl_chain` recovers the original list `l` exactly, i.e., the construction is a right inverse of `toList`.

- Claim: The head of `VTask.fromListIsChain l l_ne_nil hl` equals `l.head l_ne_nil`, the first element of the original list.

- Claim: For a two-element list `[a, b]` where `(a, b) ∈ r`, the resulting `RelSeries` has length 1, with first element `a` and last element `b`.

### Boundaries

- The list must be nonempty; the argument `x_ne_nil : x ≠ []` is required because `RelSeries` must have at least one element (length is a natural number and length 0 is already a single-element series). There is no construction for the empty list.
- A singleton list `[a]` is valid and produces a `RelSeries` of length 0; the chain condition is vacuously satisfied (no consecutive pairs exist).
- The length of the resulting series equals `x.length - 1` using natural number subtraction, so for any nonempty list of length `n ≥ 1`, the series has length `n - 1` and `n` elements indexed by `Fin (n - 1 + 1) = Fin n`.
- The `toList` of the resulting series is definitionally equal to the original list, so the construction is lossless.

### Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.toList`: the inverse direction, converting a `RelSeries` into a list; `VTask.fromListIsChain` goes the other way.
- `RelSeries.cons`: appends a single element to the front of an existing `RelSeries`, rather than constructing a series from an entire list.
- `List.IsChain`: the predicate on lists used as a hypothesis here; it is not itself a series constructor.

## Object

`VTask.tail` removes the first element from a relation series of positive length, producing a new relation series that begins at the second element of the original. Given a series `a₀ -r→ a₁ -r→ a₂ -r→ … -r→ aₙ`, the tail is the series `a₁ -r→ a₂ -r→ … -r→ aₙ`, which has length one less than the original.

## Signature

VTask.tail : {α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (p : RelSeries r) -> (len_pos : p.length ≠ 0) -> RelSeries r

The implicit argument `α` is the type of elements appearing in the series. The implicit argument `r` is the binary relation that consecutive elements of any `RelSeries r` must satisfy. The argument `p` is the relation series being truncated. The argument `len_pos` is a proof that `p` has positive length (i.e., that `p.length ≠ 0`), which is required because a series of length zero has no second element from which to start a tail.

## Conventions

The operation is defined only when the series has positive length; callers must supply a proof `len_pos : p.length ≠ 0`. There are no junk values — the length-zero case is excluded by the type.

## Worked examples

- Claim: For a relation series `p` with `p.length ≠ 0`, the tail has length `p.length - 1`.

- Claim: For any relation series `p` with `hp : p.length ≠ 0`, prepending `p.head` back onto `(p.tail hp)` (using the step at index 0 of `p`) recovers the original series `p`. This is expressed by the identity `(p.tail hp).cons p.head (p.step ⟨0, …⟩) = p`.

- Claim: For any relation series `p` with `hp : p.length ≠ 0`, the list representation of the tail equals the list-`tail` of `p`'s list representation: `(VTask.tail p hp).toList = p.toList.tail`.

- Claim: For any relation series `p`, element `x : α`, and proof `hx : r x p.head`, taking the tail of `p.cons x hx` recovers `p` exactly: `VTask.tail (p.cons x hx) (by simp) = p`.

## Boundaries

- The `len_pos` proof obligation strictly excludes length-zero series; the operation is not defined (or meaningful) on a singleton series (length 0, which has only one element and therefore no tail).
- When the input series has length exactly 1, the tail has length 0, i.e., it is a single-element series consisting only of the element at index 1 of the original.
- The indices in the resulting series are re-based to start at 0, so element `i` of the tail corresponds to element `i + 1` of the original series.
- The tail operation and `cons` are inverses: applying `cons` with `p.head` and the appropriate step proof to `p.tail hp` yields back `p` (see `cons_self_tail`); conversely, taking the tail of `p.cons x hx` yields `p` (see `tail_cons`).

## Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.head` — extracts the *first* element of the series as an element of `α`, not a sub-series.
- `RelSeries.cons` — *prepends* an element to a series, the left inverse of `VTask.tail`; often confused because `tail` and `cons` are mutual inverses.
- `List.tail` — the analogous operation on plain lists; `VTask.tail` operates on typed relation series with the step-validity invariant maintained, not on bare lists.

## VTask.smash

### Object

Given two composable relational series — the first ending at some element `X` and the second beginning at the same element `X` — `VTask.smash` produces a single concatenated relational series that traverses the elements of the first series in order, passes through `X`, and then continues through the elements of the second series. The resulting series has length equal to the sum of the two individual lengths, and every consecutive pair of elements in the combined series is still related by the underlying relation `r`.

### Signature

`{α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (p q : RelSeries r) -> (connect : p.last = q.head) -> RelSeries r`

The type `α` is the carrier type of the elements. The relation `r` is a binary relation on `α` that governs which consecutive pairs are permitted. The argument `p` is the first relational series, whose final element must coincide with the starting element of `q`. The argument `q` is the second relational series. The argument `connect` is a proof that the last element of `p` equals the head (first element) of `q`, which is the compatibility condition that makes concatenation well-defined.

### Conventions

The junction element `X = p.last = q.head` appears exactly once in the concatenated series, at the position separating the two halves; it is not duplicated.

### Worked examples

- Claim: If `p` has length 2 (elements `a₀, a₁, a₂`) and `q` has length 3 (elements `a₂, b₀, b₁, b₂`), then `VTask.smash p q h` has length 5.

- Claim: The head of `VTask.smash p q connect` equals the head of `p`.

- Claim: The last element of `VTask.smash p q connect` equals the last element of `q`.

- Claim: For index `i` in the first half (i.e., `i : Fin (p.length + 1)` cast into the combined index set), `VTask.smash p q connect` evaluated at that index equals `p` evaluated at `i`; this is exactly the content of `smash_castLE`.

- Claim: For index `i : Fin q.length`, `VTask.smash p q connect` evaluated at `(i.natAdd p.length).succ` equals `q i.succ`; this is the content of `smash_succ_natAdd`.

### Boundaries

- If `p` has length 0, then `p` is a single-element series, and `VTask.smash p q connect` is essentially `q` with its head relabelled by `connect`; the result has the same length as `q`.
- If `q` has length 0, similarly the result has the same length as `p`.
- Both `p` and `q` may have length 0 simultaneously, in which case `connect` forces `p.last = q.head`, and the result is again a single-element series of length 0.
- The condition `connect : p.last = q.head` is mandatory; without it the step condition at the junction cannot be verified.

### Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.append` (if it exists): a variant that may handle the junction differently or require a different compatibility hypothesis.
- Disjoint union of two series: `VTask.smash` shares the junction point rather than keeping the two series entirely separate.
- `RelSeries.tail` / `RelSeries.drop`: these shorten a series rather than extending it.

## Object

`VTask.map` is the pointwise lifting of a family of functions to dependent function types. Given a family of functions `f i : α i → β i` indexed by `i : ι`, it transforms a dependent function `a : ∀ i, α i` into a dependent function `∀ i, β i` by applying `f i` to the `i`-th component `a i`. In other words, the output at index `i` is `f i (a i)`.

## Signature

The implicit sort `ι` is the index type (or sort) over which the families are parameterised. The implicit families `α` and `β` assign a type (or sort) to each index `i : ι`. The explicit argument `f` is the family of component-wise functions, one function `f i : α i → β i` for each index `i`. The final argument is the dependent function to be transformed, assigning to each `i` an element of `α i`.

## Conventions

No special junk-value or boundary conventions are declared: the definition is total over all inputs with no degenerate edge cases requiring special treatment.

## Worked examples

- Claim: For `f i x = x + 1` (constant index type `Unit`) and `a _ = 3`, `VTask.map f a ()` equals `4`.
  ```lean
  example : VTask.map (fun (_ : Unit) (x : Nat) => x + 1) (fun _ => 3) () = 4 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: For `ι = Fin 2`, `α i = Nat`, `β i = Nat`, `f i x = x * 2`, and `a i = i.val + 1`, the result at index `0` is `2` and at index `1` is `4`.
  ```lean
  example : VTask.map (fun (_ : Fin 2) (x : Nat) => x * 2) (fun i => i.val + 1) ⟨0, by omega⟩ = 2 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.map` composed with itself corresponds to composing the component functions: for all `g : ∀ i, β i → γ i` and `f : ∀ i, α i → β i` and `a : ∀ i, α i`, `VTask.map g (VTask.map f a) = VTask.map (fun i => g i ∘ f i) a`.

- Claim: Applying `VTask.map` to the identity family `fun i x => x` returns the original function unchanged.

## Boundaries

- When `ι` is an empty type (e.g. `Empty` or `Fin 0`), the result is the unique function out of the empty index, and the transformation is vacuously the identity.
- When `α i` and `β i` coincide and each `f i` is the identity, `VTask.map f` is the identity on dependent functions.
- When `ι` is a `Prop` (a sort), `VTask.map` still makes sense as the sorts are allowed to be any universe, including `Prop`.

## Not to be confused with

- `Function.update`: modifies a dependent function at a single index, whereas `VTask.map` transforms all components simultaneously via given functions.
- The category-theoretic `Pi.map` on products in a category: that is a morphism between categorical products, not a construction on ordinary dependent function types.
- `Set.pi`: a set-theoretic construction collecting dependent tuples satisfying componentwise membership conditions, unrelated to transforming functions.

## Object

`VTask.EventuallyEq l f g` is the proposition that two functions `f` and `g` are **eventually equal** along a filter `l`: the set of points `x` at which `f x = g x` is a member of (i.e., is "large" with respect to) the filter `l`. Intuitively, `f` and `g` agree everywhere except possibly on a "negligible" set, where negligibility is determined by `l`. This is denoted `f =ᶠ[l] g` in Mathlib notation.

## Signature

`VTask.EventuallyEq : {α : Type u_1} -> {β : Type u_2} -> (l : Filter α) -> (f g : α → β) -> Prop`

The type parameters `α` and `β` are the domain and codomain types, inferred implicitly. The argument `l` is the filter on `α` that determines which subsets of the domain are considered "large" or "negligible". The arguments `f` and `g` are the two functions from `α` to `β` being compared.

## Conventions

There are no special junk-value or edge-case conventions declared for this definition: it is a universally quantified proposition over all filters and all functions, and is well-formed and meaningful in every case including degenerate ones (e.g., the bottom filter `⊥`, the top filter `⊤`, or the trivial filter on a one-element type).

## Worked examples

- Claim: For any filter `l` on `α`, every function `f : α → β` is eventually equal to itself along `l` (reflexivity: `f =ᶠ[l] f`).

- Claim: If `f = g` as functions (pointwise everywhere), then `f =ᶠ[l] g` along any filter `l`, since the set `{x | f x = g x}` is the universal set, which belongs to every filter.

- Claim: Along the principal filter `Filter.principal s` on a set `s`, two functions `f` and `g` satisfy `f =ᶠ[Filter.principal s] g` if and only if `f` and `g` agree on every point of `s`.

- Claim: Along the bottom filter `⊥` on any type, every pair of functions `f g : α → β` satisfies `f =ᶠ[⊥] g`, since every set belongs to `⊥`.

- Claim: Along the neighbourhood filter `𝓝 x` at a point `x` in a topological space, `f =ᶠ[𝓝 x] g` means there exists an open neighbourhood of `x` on which `f` and `g` coincide.

## Boundaries

- **Bottom filter `⊥`**: Since every set belongs to the bottom filter, `f =ᶠ[⊥] g` holds for all `f` and `g`, regardless of whether they agree anywhere.
- **Top filter `⊤` (the cofinite filter or `Filter.atTop`)**: The condition becomes more restrictive; for the top filter (principal filter of the whole set / `univ`), `f =ᶠ[⊤] g` requires `f = g` pointwise everywhere.
- **Principal filter `Filter.principal s`**: `f =ᶠ[Filter.principal s] g` if and only if `f` and `g` agree on all of `s` (the agreement set must contain `s`).
- **Codomain without decidable equality**: The proposition is still well-formed; no decidability is required since `VTask.EventuallyEq` is a `Prop`.
- **Empty type `α`**: When `α` is empty there are no functions from `α` to `β` (or only the vacuous one), and the condition holds vacuously.

## Not to be confused with

- **`Filter.Eventually` (`∀ᶠ x in l, p x`)**: The underlying "eventually" quantifier for a predicate; `VTask.EventuallyEq l f g` is the special case where the predicate is `fun x => f x = g x`.
- **`Filter.EventuallyLE` (`f ≤ᶠ[l] g`)**: The analogous notion for eventual inequality (ordering), where `{x | f x ≤ g x} ∈ l`; weaker than eventual equality.
- **Pointwise equality `f = g`**: Full function extensionality; it implies `f =ᶠ[l] g` for any `l`, but is strictly stronger (eventual equality allows disagreement on a filter-negligible set).

## Object

A function `f : α → β` is *antiperiodic with antiperiod `c`* if shifting every input by `c` negates the output: for every element `x` of `α`, the value of `f` at `x + c` equals the negation of `f` at `x`. Antiperiodicity is a strict strengthening of periodicity: applying the shift twice recovers the original value (since negating twice is the identity when negation is involutive), so an antiperiodic function is automatically periodic with period `2c`.

Classic examples include the real sine and cosine functions, each antiperiodic with antiperiod `π`, and the complex exponential, antiperiodic with antiperiod `π * I`.

## Signature

`VTask.Antiperiodic : {α : Type u_1} -> {β : Type u_2} -> [Add α] -> [Neg β] -> (f : α → β) -> (c : α) -> Prop`

The type `α` is the domain of `f`; it must carry an addition so that `x + c` makes sense. The type `β` is the codomain; it must carry a negation so that `-f x` makes sense. The argument `f` is the function being tested for antiperiodicity. The argument `c` is the proposed antiperiod — the shift amount whose repeated application negates the output.

## Conventions

There are no special junk-value or edge-case conventions declared for this predicate; it is a straightforward universally quantified proposition, and the only vacuous special case arises from whatever algebraic structure `α` and `β` happen to carry.

## Worked examples

- Claim: The real sine function satisfies `VTask.Antiperiodic Real.sin Real.pi`, meaning `sin(x + π) = -sin x` for all real `x`.

- Claim: The real cosine function satisfies `VTask.Antiperiodic Real.cos Real.pi`, meaning `cos(x + π) = -cos x` for all real `x`.

- Claim: For any `f : α → β` and `c : α`, if `VTask.Antiperiodic f c` holds, then in particular `f c = -f 0` (obtained by specialising the universal statement to `x = 0`).

- Claim: If `VTask.Antiperiodic f c` holds and `f 0 = 0`, then for every natural number `n`, `f (n * c) = 0`.

## Boundaries

- When `c = 0` (in a type where `0` exists), antiperiodicity collapses to the requirement `f x = -f x` for all `x`, which forces `f` to be identically zero in any type where `a = -a` implies `a = 0` (e.g. any additive group of odd order, or any `CharZero` group).
- Antiperiodicity is defined for any types with `Add` and `Neg`; no ring, group, or module structure is required beyond these two operations. Many consequences require stronger algebraic assumptions.
- An antiperiodic function is periodic with period `2c` whenever the negation is involutive (i.e. `- -a = a`), but the predicate itself does not assert or require this.
- The predicate makes no assumption that `c ≠ 0`.

## Not to be confused with

- *Periodicity* (`∀ x, f (x + c) = f x`): periodicity requires the values to repeat, not negate; antiperiodicity is strictly stronger in that it reverses sign.
- *Odd functions* (`∀ x, f (-x) = -f x`): odd symmetry is about negating the *input*, while antiperiodicity is about *shifting* the input by a fixed amount.
- *Antiperiodic with period `2c`*: sometimes writers call `2c` the "antiperiod"; here `c` is the half-period (the shift that negates), not the full period.

## Object

`VTask.Forall p l` is the proposition that the predicate `p` holds for every element of the list `l`. It is the conjunction of `p a` over all elements `a` of `l`, unfolded structurally: for example, `VTask.Forall p [a, b, c]` is exactly `p a ∧ p b ∧ p c`, and `VTask.Forall p []` is `True`.

## Signature

`VTask.Forall : {α : Type u_1} -> (p : α → Prop) -> List α → Prop`

The implicit argument `α` is the element type. The argument `p` is the predicate to be tested against each element of the list. The final argument is the list whose elements are tested.

## Conventions

When the list is empty, `VTask.Forall p []` is defined to be `True` (the empty conjunction), reflecting the vacuous truth of a universal statement over an empty collection.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) [1, 2, 3]` is equivalent to `1 < 10 ∧ 2 < 10 ∧ 3 < 10`.

- Claim: `VTask.Forall (fun n => n < 10) []` is `True` (empty conjunction).

- Claim: `VTask.Forall p [x]` is definitionally equal to `p x` (singleton list gives no conjunction wrapper).

- Claim: `VTask.Forall p l` is equivalent to `∀ a ∈ l, p a`.

## Boundaries

- **Empty list**: `VTask.Forall p [] = True`. There are no elements to check, so the result is vacuously true.
- **Singleton list**: `VTask.Forall p [x] = p x`. A single-element list unfolds directly to `p x`, with no `∧ True` padding.
- **Two or more elements**: `VTask.Forall p (x :: l) = p x ∧ VTask.Forall p l` (for `l` nonempty); the result is a right-nested conjunction.
- **Implication**: If `VTask.Forall p l` holds and `p x → q x` for all `x`, then `VTask.Forall q l` holds (monotonicity in the predicate).

## Not to be confused with

- `List.Forall₂`: a relation between *two* lists of possibly different types, checking a binary predicate pairwise, not a unary predicate on a single list.
- `∀ a ∈ l, p a`: the standard bounded universal quantifier; equivalent in meaning but does not unfold to a bare conjunction structure.
- `List.all`: a boolean-valued function testing a decidable predicate on every list element, not a `Prop`-valued conjunction.

## Object

The hyperoperation sequence is a family of binary operations on natural numbers that extends the familiar hierarchy of addition, multiplication, and exponentiation to arbitrarily high levels. The `n`th hyperoperation applied to `m` and `k` is written `VTask.hyperoperation n m k` and formalises the idea that each level is iterated application of the level below: level 0 is the successor function, level 1 is addition, level 2 is multiplication, level 3 is exponentiation, level 4 is tetration (iterated exponentiation), and so on.

## Signature

`VTask.hyperoperation : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`

The first argument `n` is the *level* (or rank) of the hyperoperation — 0 for successor, 1 for addition, 2 for multiplication, 3 for exponentiation, and higher values for the iterated tower operations beyond exponentiation. The second argument `m` is the *left operand* (the base in the exponential and tetration regime). The third argument `k` is the *right operand* (the exponent, or the height of the tower, in the higher regimes).

## Conventions

At level 0, the left operand `m` is completely ignored and the result is always `k + 1` (pure successor). At level 1 with right operand 0, the result is `m` (addition identity: `m + 0 = m`). At level 2 with right operand 0, the result is `0` (multiplication identity: `m * 0 = 0`). For every level 3 and above with right operand 0, the result is `1` (the identity element for exponentiation and all higher operations). These base cases reflect the standard mathematical convention for the hyperoperation sequence and make each level a left-iterated application of the level below, starting from the appropriate identity.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 0 999 5 = 6` — at level 0 (successor), the left operand is irrelevant and the result is `5 + 1 = 6`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 1 3 4 = 7` — level 1 is addition, and `3 + 4 = 7`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 2 5 3 = 15` — level 2 is multiplication, and `5 × 3 = 15`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 3 2 10 = 1024` — level 3 is exponentiation, and `2^10 = 1024`.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 16` — level 4 is tetration; `2 ↑↑ 3 = 2^(2^2) = 2^4 = 16` (using the recursion: `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 1 = 2`, `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 2 = 4`, `VTask.hyperoperation 4 2 3 = 2^4 = 16`).

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 5 1 100 = 1` — for level ≥ 3, base `m = 1` always yields 1 regardless of the right operand.

- Claim: `VTask.hyperoperation 7 2 2 = 4` — for any level ≥ 1, `VTask.hyperoperation n 2 2 = 4`.

## Boundaries

- **Level 0**: The left operand is completely ignored. `VTask.hyperoperation 0 m k = k + 1` for all `m` and `k`.
- **Right operand 0 at level 1**: Returns `m` (addition by zero).
- **Right operand 0 at level 2**: Returns `0` (multiplication by zero).
- **Right operand 0 at level ≥ 3**: Returns `1` (the multiplicative/exponential identity).
- **Left operand 1 at level ≥ 3**: Always returns 1, since iterating exponentiation of 1 stays at 1.
- **Left operand 0 at level ≥ 4**: `VTask.hyperoperation (n+4) 0 k` equals `1` when `k` is even and `0` when `k` is odd, reflecting the alternating pattern of iterated exponentiation with base 0.
- **Any level, base 2, right operand 2**: Always returns 4 for level ≥ 1 (since `2+2=4`, `2×2=4`, `2^2=4`, `2↑↑2=4`, etc.).

## Not to be confused with

- **`Nat.pow`** (exponentiation): This is the special case `VTask.hyperoperation 3 m k = m ^ k`; `Nat.pow` handles only one level of the hierarchy.
- **`Nat.succ`** (the successor function): This is the special case `VTask.hyperoperation 0 m k = k + 1`; the left operand plays no role at level 0.
- **Ackermann function**: Closely related to the hyperoperation sequence (the Ackermann function can be expressed in terms of hyperoperations), but is a distinct two-argument function with a different indexing convention.

## VTask.fromListIsChain

### Object

Given a nonempty list whose consecutive elements are related by a binary relation `r`, `VTask.fromListIsChain` produces a `RelSeries r` — a finite sequence of elements of a type `α` in which each consecutive pair is in the relation `r`. The length of the resulting series is one less than the length of the input list (since a series of length `n` has `n+1` elements, matching a list of `n+1` elements). This constructor is essentially the inverse of converting a `RelSeries` to a list.

### Signature

VTask.fromListIsChain : {α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (x : List α) -> (x_ne_nil : x ≠ []) -> (hx : List.IsChain (fun x1 x2 => (x1, x2) ∈ r) x) -> RelSeries r

The implicit argument `α` is the element type. The implicit argument `r` is the binary relation on `α`, presented as a set of pairs. The first explicit argument `x` is the input list of elements of `α`. The second explicit argument `x_ne_nil` is a proof that the list is nonempty (i.e., not the empty list). The third explicit argument `hx` is a proof that consecutive elements in `x` are related by `r` — that is, `x` forms a chain under `r`.

### Conventions

There are no junk-value or out-of-domain edge conventions to declare: the function is total over all inputs satisfying the stated hypotheses, and the hypotheses themselves (nonemptiness and the chain condition) are required arguments rather than silently handled edge cases.

### Worked examples

- Claim: For a singleton list `[a]`, `VTask.fromListIsChain [a] _ _` has length 0 (a series with a single element).

- Claim: For a two-element list `[a, b]` where `(a, b) ∈ r`, `VTask.fromListIsChain [a, b] _ _` has length 1.

- Claim: The `toList` of `VTask.fromListIsChain l l_ne_nil hl` equals `l` — that is, converting the constructed series back to a list recovers the original list.

- Claim: The head of `VTask.fromListIsChain l l_ne_nil hl` equals the head of `l` — the first element of the series coincides with the first element of the input list.

- Claim: If `x ~[r] (l.head l_ne_nil)`, then `VTask.fromListIsChain (x :: l) _ _` equals `(VTask.fromListIsChain l l_ne_nil hl).cons x _` — prepending an element respects the `cons` operation on series.

### Boundaries

- **Singleton list**: A list of exactly one element vacuously satisfies the chain condition (there are no consecutive pairs to relate), and the resulting `RelSeries` has length 0. This is the minimal case.
- **Two-element list**: Requires exactly one proof obligation: that the first and second elements are related. The resulting series has length 1.
- **Length relationship**: The `RelSeries` produced always has `length = List.length x - 1`. Since `x` is nonempty, `List.length x ≥ 1`, so this is always a natural number (no underflow issues).
- **Round-trip**: The construction is a right inverse of `toList`: applying `toList` to the result always recovers the original list `x`.

### Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.toList`: The reverse direction — converts an existing `RelSeries` into a list; `fromListIsChain` goes the other way.
- `RelSeries.cons`: Prepends a single element to an existing `RelSeries`, rather than constructing one from a whole list at once.
- `List.IsChain`: The chain condition used as a hypothesis here, which only asserts the consecutive-relation property on a list but does not itself produce a `RelSeries`.

## Object

`VTask.tail` takes a relation series `a₀ -r→ a₁ -r→ a₂ -r→ … -r→ aₙ` of positive length and returns the shorter relation series `a₁ -r→ a₂ -r→ … -r→ aₙ` obtained by dropping the first element. The resulting series has length one less than the original.

## Signature

The implicit argument `α` is the type of elements appearing in the series, and `r` is the binary relation (of type `SetRel α α`) that consecutive elements must satisfy. The argument `p` is the relation series being operated on; it is a sequence `a₀, a₁, …, aₙ` of length `n` where each consecutive pair satisfies `r`. The argument `len_pos` is a proof that `p`'s length is nonzero (i.e., `p.length ≠ 0`), guaranteeing there is at least one step and thus a well-defined second element to serve as the new head.

## Conventions

The length of the returned series is `p.length - 1` (natural-number subtraction, which is safe here because `len_pos` ensures the length is at least 1). The element at index `i` of the tail series is the element at index `i + 1` of the original series, so the head of the tail is `p.toFun 1`.

## Worked examples

- Claim: For a series of length 3 with elements `[a, b, c, d]`, `(VTask.tail p hp).length = 2`.

- Claim: Prepending the head of `p` back onto `VTask.tail p hp` (with the first step of `p` as the connecting relation witness) recovers the original series `p` — that is, `(VTask.tail p hp).cons p.head (p.step ⟨0, _⟩) = p`.

- Claim: For a series `p` obtained by `q.cons x hx`, the tail of `p` is again `q` — that is, `VTask.tail (q.cons x hx) (by simp) = q`.

- Claim: The list representation of `VTask.tail p hp` equals the tail (in the `List` sense) of the list representation of `p` — that is, `(VTask.tail p hp).toList = p.toList.tail`.

## Boundaries

- The `len_pos` proof is required and cannot be omitted: a series of length 0 consists of a single element with no steps, so there is no second element to serve as the new head, and `tail` is not defined in that case.
- When `p.length = 1` (a single step `a₀ -r→ a₁`), the tail has length 0, which is a valid relation series consisting solely of the element `a₁` with no steps.
- Natural-number subtraction `p.length - 1` is exact (not lossy) here because `len_pos` guarantees `p.length ≥ 1`.

## Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.head`: extracts the *first* element of a series as a single value, not a sub-series.
- `RelSeries.cons`: the inverse operation — prepends an element to an existing series, increasing length by 1; `tail` and `cons` are mutual inverses (as witnessed by `cons_self_tail` and `tail_cons`).
- `List.tail`: the analogous operation on plain lists, which is related (their list representations coincide) but operates on a structurally simpler type with no relation constraint.
