## Object

`VTask.smash` concatenates two finite relational series end-to-end into a single longer series. Given a series `p` whose last element equals the first element (head) of a series `q`, it produces a new series whose elements are precisely those of `p` followed by those of `q` (with the shared junction point appearing only once), and whose steps inherit all the relational steps from both `p` and `q`.

## Signature

```
VTask.smash : {α : Type u_1} -> {r : SetRel α α} -> (p q : RelSeries r) -> (connect : p.last = q.head) -> RelSeries r
```

The implicit type argument `α` is the carrier type of the series elements. The implicit argument `r` is the binary relation that consecutive elements must satisfy. The explicit argument `p` is the left (earlier) series ending at some element `X`. The explicit argument `q` is the right (later) series beginning at the same element `X`. The argument `connect` is a proof that the last element of `p` coincides with the head of `q`, which is the compatibility condition required to join the two series at their shared junction.

## Conventions

The junction element `X = p.last = q.head` appears exactly once in the combined series — it is not duplicated. The length of the resulting series equals `p.length + q.length` (each length counts the number of steps, so the number of elements is one more than the length, and the shared endpoint contributes only once to the combined count).

## Worked examples

- Claim: For two length-1 series `p` and `q` that share their junction, `VTask.smash p q h` has length 2.

- Claim: The values of `VTask.smash p q h` on indices drawn from `p`'s range coincide with the values of `p`. Specifically, for any `i : Fin (p.length + 1)`, `(VTask.smash p q h) (i.castLE _) = p i`.

- Claim: The values of `VTask.smash p q h` on indices drawn from `q`'s interior (strictly after the junction) coincide with the corresponding values of `q`. Specifically, for `i : Fin q.length`, `(VTask.smash p q h) (i.natAdd p.length).succ = q i.succ`.

- Claim: For `i : Fin p.length`, `(VTask.smash p q h) (i.castAdd q.length).succ = p i.succ`, so the successor-of-castAdd indexing correctly retrieves elements from `p`.

## Boundaries

- If `p` has length 0 (a single-element series), `smash p q h` is essentially a copy of `q`, resting on the fact that `p`'s unique element equals `q`'s head.
- If `q` has length 0 (a single-element series), `smash p q h` is essentially a copy of `p`, with the junction element being `q`'s sole element.
- If both `p` and `q` have length 0, the result is still a valid length-0 series (a single element), provided the connect condition holds — meaning `p.last = q.head` forces both to carry the same element.
- The connect condition is essential: the operation is not defined (and not meaningful) when `p.last ≠ q.head`; the caller must supply a proof.

## Not to be confused with

- `RelSeries.append`: A conceptually similar operation in some libraries that may duplicate the junction point or use different index conventions — `VTask.smash` specifically avoids duplication of the shared element.
- `RelSeries.cons` / `RelSeries.snoc`: Operations that prepend or append a single element with a single relational step, as opposed to joining two entire series.
- Disjoint union of series: A construction that would keep both series separate rather than gluing them at a shared point.

## Object

Given a dependent type family indexed by `ι`, `VTask.map` is the operation that lifts a family of functions `f i : α i → β i` (one for each index `i`) to a function between dependent function spaces: it takes a dependent function `a : ∀ i, α i` and produces a new dependent function `∀ i, β i` whose `i`-th component is `f i (a i)`. In other words, it applies each fibrewise function `f i` to the corresponding component of the input section.

## Signature

`VTask.map : {ι : Sort u_1} -> {α : ι → Sort u_2} -> {β : ι → Sort u_3} -> (f : (i : ι) → α i → β i) -> ((i : ι) → α i) → (i : ι) → β i`

The implicit argument `ι` is the index type (or sort) over which the dependent functions range. The implicit argument `α` is the source type family, assigning to each `i : ι` a type `α i`. The implicit argument `β` is the target type family, assigning to each `i : ι` a type `β i`. The explicit argument `f` is the family of fibrewise functions: for each index `i`, `f i` maps `α i` to `β i`. The next argument is a dependent function (a global section) of `α`, and the result is a dependent function (a global section) of `β`.

## Conventions

No special junk-value or edge conventions are declared for this definition: it is a total, universally-quantified construction with no cases where the output is left undefined or assigned an arbitrary value.

## Worked examples

- Claim: Applying `VTask.map` with `f i := Nat.succ` (for a constant index type `Unit`) to the constant section `fun _ => 3` yields the section `fun _ => 4`.
  ```lean
  example : VTask.map (fun (_ : Unit) (n : Nat) => Nat.succ n) (fun _ => 3) () = 4 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: Applying `VTask.map` with `f i := Nat.add i` to the section `fun i => i` (over `Fin 3`) yields the section `fun i => i + i`, so in particular the value at index `2` is `4`.
  ```lean
  example : VTask.map (fun (i : Fin 3) (n : Nat) => i.val + n) (fun i => i.val) ⟨2, by omega⟩ = 4 := by decide
  ```

- Claim: `VTask.map` composes correctly: applying `VTask.map g` after `VTask.map f` is the same as `VTask.map (fun i => g i ∘ f i)`. That is, for any `a : ∀ i, α i`, `VTask.map g (VTask.map f a) = VTask.map (fun i x => g i (f i x)) a`.

- Claim: `VTask.map` preserves `Function.update`: if `g : ∀ i, α i`, `i₀ : ι`, and `a : α i₀`, then applying `VTask.map f` to `Function.update g i₀ a` equals `Function.update (VTask.map f g) i₀ (f i₀ a)`.

## Boundaries

- When `ι` is the empty type (or has no inhabitants), the input and output dependent functions are vacuously defined; `VTask.map f a` is also vacuously defined and the result is the unique function out of the empty type.
- When `ι` is a singleton type (e.g., `Unit`), `VTask.map f a` simply applies `f ()` to `a ()`, reducing to ordinary function application.
- When all the `f i` are identity functions, `VTask.map f a = a` for any section `a`.
- When `α` and `β` are both constant families (i.e., `α i = A` and `β i = B` for all `i`), `VTask.map` reduces to ordinary post-composition by `f i` in the non-dependent sense.

## Not to be confused with

- The category-theoretic `Pi.map` on products of objects in a category: that operates on morphisms between categorical products, not on dependent function types in `Sort`.
- `Function.comp`: which composes two ordinary (non-dependent, single-index) functions rather than lifting a family of fibrewise maps to sections.
- `Finset.map` or `List.map`: which apply a single function to each element of a finite collection, rather than lifting a family of type-varying functions across a dependent Pi type.

## Object

A natural number `n` is **perfect** if it equals the sum of all its proper divisors (i.e., all positive divisors strictly less than `n`), provided `n` itself is positive. The prototypical examples are 6 (proper divisors 1, 2, 3; sum = 6) and 28 (proper divisors 1, 2, 4, 7, 14; sum = 28).

## Signature

`VTask.Perfect : (n : ℕ) -> Prop`

The sole argument `n` is the natural number being tested for perfection.

## Conventions

The number 0 is explicitly excluded from being perfect: the definition requires `0 < n` as a conjunct, so `VTask.Perfect 0` is false by convention even though the empty sum of proper divisors of 0 would vacuously equal 0.

## Worked Examples

- Claim: `VTask.Perfect 6` holds, because the proper divisors of 6 are 1, 2, 3, which sum to 6, and 6 > 0.

- Claim: `VTask.Perfect 28` holds, because the proper divisors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, which sum to 28, and 28 > 0.

- Claim: `¬ VTask.Perfect 1` holds, because the only proper divisor sum for 1 is 0 (there are no proper divisors), which does not equal 1.

- Claim: `¬ VTask.Perfect 0` holds, because the positivity condition `0 < 0` fails.

- Claim: For any prime `p`, `¬ VTask.Perfect p` holds, because the only proper divisor of a prime is 1, and no prime equals 1.

- Claim: For every positive nonzero `n`, exactly one of `VTask.Perfect n`, `Nat.Deficient n`, `Nat.Abundant n` holds.

## Boundaries

- **n = 0**: Not perfect by definition (the positivity clause `0 < n` fails). This is a deliberate junk-value convention.
- **n = 1**: Not perfect; the proper divisors of 1 form an empty set, so their sum is 0, which is not equal to 1.
- **Prime numbers**: Never perfect, since the only proper divisor of a prime `p` is 1, and no prime equals 1.
- **Even perfect numbers**: The even perfect numbers are completely characterised (Euclid–Euler theorem); whether odd perfect numbers exist is an open problem, but the definition itself places no parity restriction.
- **Characterisation via full divisor sum**: For positive `n`, being perfect is equivalent to the sum of *all* divisors (including `n` itself) equalling `2 * n`.

## Not to be Confused With

- **`Nat.Abundant`**: A positive `n` is abundant when the sum of its proper divisors *exceeds* `n`; contrast with perfect, where equality holds.
- **`Nat.Deficient`**: A positive `n` is deficient when the sum of its proper divisors is *less than* `n`; together with abundant and perfect these three cases partition the positive naturals.
- **`Nat.Pseudoperfect`**: A weaker notion where `n` equals the sum of *some subset* of its proper divisors (not necessarily all of them); every perfect number is pseudoperfect, but not conversely.

## VTask.toSimpleGraphStrict

### Object

Given a directed graph `G` on a vertex type `V`, `VTask.toSimpleGraphStrict G` is the simple (undirected) graph on `V` whose edges are exactly the *bidirectional* arcs of `G`: two distinct vertices `v` and `w` are adjacent in the result if and only if `G` contains both the arc from `v` to `w` and the arc from `w` to `v`. One-way arcs are discarded entirely.

### Signature

The sole argument `G` is the directed graph being converted. The vertex type `V` is implicit, inferred from `G`.

### Conventions

Because `SimpleGraph` in Mathlib requires irreflexivity by construction, the adjacency relation of the resulting graph is automatically irreflexive (a vertex is never adjacent to itself), even though the distinctness condition `v ≠ w` is imposed explicitly as part of the definition.

### Worked examples

- Claim: For any digraph `G`, if `G.toSimpleGraphStrict` declares `v` and `w` adjacent, then both directed arcs `G.Adj v w` and `G.Adj w v` hold and `v ≠ w`.

- Claim: On the complete digraph `⊤ : Digraph V`, every pair of distinct vertices has both directed arcs present, so `(⊤ : Digraph V).toSimpleGraphStrict = ⊤` (the complete simple graph).

- Claim: On the empty digraph `⊥ : Digraph V`, no arcs exist in either direction, so `(⊥ : Digraph V).toSimpleGraphStrict = ⊥` (the empty simple graph).

- Claim: `VTask.toSimpleGraphStrict` is monotone: if `G ≤ H` as digraphs (meaning every arc of `G` is also an arc of `H`), then `G.toSimpleGraphStrict ≤ H.toSimpleGraphStrict` as simple graphs.

- Claim: `G.toSimpleGraphStrict` is a subgraph of the "inclusive" orientation-forgetting map that places an undirected edge whenever *at least one* directed arc is present.

### Boundaries

- A directed arc `G.Adj v w` with no reverse arc `G.Adj w v` contributes **no** edge to the result; only mutually-oriented pairs survive.
- If `V` has fewer than two elements, the result is necessarily the empty simple graph, since no two distinct vertices exist.
- The empty digraph maps to the empty simple graph; the complete digraph maps to the complete simple graph.

### Not to be confused with

- `Digraph.toSimpleGraphInclusive`: the "inclusive" (or "underlying") undirected graph that adds an edge whenever *either* directed arc is present; `toSimpleGraphStrict` is a subgraph of this.
- `SimpleGraph.toDigraph` or orientation maps: these go in the opposite direction, turning an undirected graph into a digraph, rather than collapsing a digraph to a simple graph.
- `Digraph.Adj` itself: the raw directed adjacency relation, which is not symmetric and does not produce a `SimpleGraph`.

## Object

`VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ s` is the proposition that two functions `f₁` and `f₂` from a type `α` to a type `β` agree pointwise on every element of the subset `s ⊆ α`. That is, for every `x` belonging to `s`, the values `f₁ x` and `f₂ x` are equal. Outside of `s`, the functions may differ arbitrarily.

## Signature

`VTask.EqOn : {α : Type u} -> {β : Type v} -> (f₁ f₂ : α → β) -> (s : Set α) -> Prop`

The universe levels `u` and `v` are implicit and inferred from context. `f₁` is the first function being compared; `f₂` is the second function being compared. `s` is the subset of the common domain `α` on which pointwise equality is required.

## Conventions

No special junk-value or boundary conventions are declared for this definition: it is a universally-quantified proposition with no partiality — when `s` is empty the proposition holds vacuously for any two functions, and no sentinel values are involved.

## Worked examples

- Claim: `VTask.EqOn (fun n : ℕ => n + 0) (fun n : ℕ => n) Set.univ` holds, since adding zero is the identity on natural numbers.

- Claim: `VTask.EqOn (fun n : ℕ => n * 2) (fun n : ℕ => n + n) {1, 2, 3}` holds, since doubling equals self-addition at every natural number, and in particular at 1, 2, and 3.

- Claim: `VTask.EqOn (fun _ : ℕ => 0) (fun _ : ℕ => 1) (∅ : Set ℕ)` holds vacuously because the domain set is empty.

- Claim: `¬ VTask.EqOn (fun n : ℕ => n) (fun n : ℕ => n + 1) {0}` holds because the two functions differ at 0.

## Boundaries

- **Empty set**: When `s = ∅`, `VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ ∅` is vacuously true for any `f₁` and `f₂`, regardless of how they differ globally.
- **Universal set**: When `s = Set.univ`, `VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ Set.univ` is equivalent to `f₁ = f₂` as functions (by function extensionality), since equality is required at every point.
- **Monotonicity**: If `VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ t` and `s ⊆ t`, then `VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ s`, so the predicate is antitone in the set argument.
- **Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity**: The predicate is an equivalence relation on functions relative to any fixed set `s`.

## Not to be confused with

- `Function.funext_iff` / global function equality: `f₁ = f₂` requires agreement at *all* points, whereas `VTask.EqOn f₁ f₂ s` only requires agreement on the subset `s`.
- `Set.EqOn` restricted to a subtype: one might manually restrict functions to a subtype and then ask for equality; `VTask.EqOn` avoids subtype construction by working with a set predicate directly.
- `Set.SurjOn` / `Set.MapsTo`: these describe relational properties of a single function between sets, whereas `VTask.EqOn` compares two functions pointwise on a set.

## 1. Object

A function `f : α → β` is **even** if it is symmetric under negation of its argument: for every element `x` in the domain, applying `f` to the negation of `x` yields the same result as applying `f` to `x` itself. This is the abstract, algebraic generalisation of the familiar notion from real analysis where an even function satisfies `f(−x) = f(x)` for all real `x`.

## 2. Signature

The implicit type argument `α` is the domain type, which must carry a negation operation (supplied by the `Neg α` instance). The implicit type `β` is the codomain type, which needs no additional structure. The explicit argument `f` is the function under scrutiny — the one being tested for evenness.

## 3. Conventions

No special junk-value or boundary conventions are declared: the property is a universally-quantified statement over all elements of the domain, and every domain element is treated uniformly. There are no distinguished inputs that receive special treatment.

## 4. Worked examples

- Claim: Every constant function `fun _ : α ↦ b` satisfies `VTask.Even (fun _ : α ↦ b)`, because the output does not depend on the argument at all.

- Claim: The function `fun x : ℤ ↦ x * x` (squaring on the integers) satisfies `VTask.Even (fun x : ℤ ↦ x * x)`, since `(−x)² = x²` for all integers.

- Claim: If `f` and `g` are both even functions `α → β` (with `β` having addition), then their pointwise sum `f + g` is also even, as `(f + g)(−x) = f(−x) + g(−x) = f(x) + g(x) = (f + g)(x)`.

- Claim: The zero function `fun (_ : α) ↦ (0 : β)` satisfies `VTask.Even (fun _ : α ↦ (0 : β))` whenever `β` has a zero.

## 5. Boundaries

- When the domain type `α` has only one element, every function on it is trivially even, since there is nothing to check beyond `f(−⋆) = f(⋆)`, which holds by reflexivity as long as negation is the identity.
- When `α` is a type where negation is the identity (e.g., a type with `−x = x` for all `x`), every function is automatically even.
- The property makes no requirement on the codomain `β` beyond being a type; in particular `β` need not have negation, zero, or any algebraic structure.
- A function that is both even and odd (in the sense of `VTask.Odd`) need not be the zero function unless additional structure (such as `2` being invertible) is present.

## 6. Not to be confused with

- `VTask.Odd`: the companion property `f(−x) = −f(x)` for all `x`, which requires negation on the *codomain* and is the opposite parity class.
- `Even : α → Prop` (the predicate on elements): states that a single element of a type is even (divisible by 2), completely unrelated to symmetry of functions.
- Symmetry of a binary relation or a bilinear form: those notions of "even" or "symmetric" concern two-argument maps, not the negation-symmetry of a one-argument function.
